Question: As a surgeon, have you opened somebody up only to realise that they were beyond saving?
Old_Answer: Unfortunately, yes. There was this patient, 55 year old guy. He came with acute abdominal pain. The patient was in severe distress and the vitals weren’t good even at presentation. He was way too unstable to get a CT scan so we went ahead with just an Ultrasound. Ultrasound wasn’t very conclusive but it suggested intestinal obstruction. The patient was just getting worse and worse so we gave him initial resuscitation and decided to open him. We were prepared to face unexpected scenarios. But we weren’t prepared for what it actually was. As soon as we entered the abdominal cavity, copious amounts of reddish liquid oozed out. A little deeper and there it was..about 80% of his stomach, duodenum, the entire small intestine a portion of ascending and transverse colon were almost black in colour. Every surgeon’s arch nemesis…Superior Mesentric Artery thrombosis. But in this case Stomach was also involved. Basically, the blood supply to his stomach and his entire small intestine and parts of large intestine was compromised. Due to this the parts were ischaemic. There is nothing you can do in this situation. If there was enough healthy gut remaining we would have just cut out the dead part and anastomosed the healthy parts. There just wasn’t enough healthy gut here. So we just closed the patient up, informed the relatives and sent the patient back to the ICU where he passed away a few hours later, surrounded by his family. It’s very disheartening for a surgeon to accept there’s nothing you can do for the patient in front of you. But then, a good surgeon knows when to cut but the best ones know when not to. Just operating when we knew he wouldn’t survive the procedure would have led to him dying on the table. Atleast by closing him up he could pass away surrounded by his family. And believe me, that matters. That matters to the patient and that matters to the family. And while I was heartbroken at losing my patient, it gave me the tiniest bit of satisfaction knowing that we could give that family the last few hours with him. And, hopefully, we could give them closure. P.S. So, a lot of you are interested in the risk factors and how to diagnose the condition. Here’s an article that explains SMA thrombosis is simple terms by Eduardo Franca; Maxim E. Shaydakov; Jason Kosove.

What is not easy is sitting together and talking about the unpleasant, finding a solution no matter how messy, helping the other person get back on their feet, catching your partner from falling because we all slip up sometimes! Question: Does anyone want to write their heart out here?
Old_Answer: I want to. I need to. I'm in horrible pain. I lost a patient today. I mean, our unit lost a patient today. I admitted him in the casualty, I was the one who talked to his family, I was also the one who wrote his death certificate. I know my job comes with the responsibility of dealing with death. But what if you think that death is your fault? What if I was more cautious? What if I had suggested more aggressive treatment? What if, what if, what if? He just looked so fine. No distress, no pain and suddenly he went into shock. Neither me, nor any of the consultants thought of anything this serious. Medical science is a mystery and sometimes it throws such googlies. Mistakes happen. But I just hate the fact that my mistakes can kill people. I am aware I'm not senior enough or powerful enough yet to take any vital decisions about patient care. But even then, I can't help but wonder about all the things I could have done differently. Would they have made a difference? Who knows. May be, maybe not. We'll never know. A doctor's day is full of little joys when some patient gives a thank you note or just a smile of gratitude. But what about a bad day? Why isn't this taught in med school? What happens when things go wrong? How do you get back to work the next day when you wake up feeling like a murderer? You just do. You get humbled by the realisation that at the end of the day, you're not God. Then you get ready, put on that white coat, and march ahead. Head held high, heart just a little bit broken.

Question: What's the hardest truth of life?
Old_Answer: Death. Death is the hardest and ultimate truth of life. You can go round and round, sugarcoat it, pretend like you've any control over it but there it remains…the ultimate truth. I am a doctor, I've probably faced death more than other people. But, the realisation of the inevitability of death dawned to me after I lost my beloved grandmother. My aaji, my dad's mom. She was very very close to me. Since my mom is a working woman, my aaji had a lion's share in raising me. She was my mom. All my childhood memories are with her. She was so so proud of me. Even though she was 89, I just never thought she'll actually leave us all. Silly, I know. Naive, for sure. But, when it comes to people you love, do you actually ever want to believe they are not going to be with you forever? Her death was a massive shock to me, it's been 6 months and I still can't get over it. The idea that I will never hear her call me 'baudi' makes me heartbroken. The fact that I may one day forget her voice crushes me. When my grandmother was sick, I kind of downplayed it. I had that arrogance that she'll fight it all, we'll fight it all. My dad's a doctor, so am I and most of our friends. Aaji was so strong, one illness can't do her any harm. But when that unfortunate moment came, none of us could do anything. We just had to see her go. There was no rhyme or reason. There was no coming back from there. As much as I miss her every moment, nothing anyone can do can bring her back. And every single life has to face death, some sooner, some later. But it's inevitable. It's that inevitability of death that makes life so precious. That's where it ends. Life ends in the ultimate truth.. death.

Question: What are the weirdest reasons to reject a prospective bride/groom in an arranged marriage?
Old_Answer: This is about my elder sister. She's a lawyer and has completed visharad in music (it's a degree in classical music/dance that you get after 7 long years of practice). So after she turned 23, my parents started searching for a groom for her. A lot of prospects rejected because she's into music! Seriously! Girls from reputed families don't sing you see! And this isn't even the weirdest reason. There was this one guy. He had done BCom and was working for his father. Which is fine, we had no problem since his family seemed really nice. So my parents and sister went to their city, they had come with like 10 people. Parents and the guy and his brother, sister in law, uncles and aunts. All of them, at an expensive restaurant obviously at my parents' expense. My sister has glasses, so do I. But that day she was wearing lenses. But she didn't think it is a big deal so while she was talking with that guy at another table she mentioned it to him. My parents and sister came home. They dint really like the family much, a bit too orthodox compared to my family. They called us back after a couple of days. They rejected my sister. Reason- she has glasses! What?! I mean, what?! Apparently they din't want their future grandchildren to have glasses! And his father told this to my father. My father is an ophthalmologist! Genetics is one of a million other causes for short sightedness. Baba told this to his father, also said we're not interested either! He somehow calmly cut the call. Of all the weird reasons I have heard, this seemed really really shallow. I mean, this was 2011 not 1900s!
